_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 6 Forces Change Things. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. The chapters follow LESSON["lecture"] in content/lesson-6.py part by part, under its own headings and in its own words: the still ball that is kicked, pushed along, pushed back and tapped on the side; the toy car pushed gently, medium and hard (3, 6 and 9 steps) on the lesson's own track (ART.sim pushBall); the results table and the block graph the child builds next; the sponge, the metal paperclip and the wooden block of the shape test (the block's push too small to change it, as the lesson says); and the rolling ball that the floor slows and the wall stops.
title: Forces Change Things
subtitle: Grade 2 Science
objectives: Know that forces can change the movement of an object.
Know that forces can change the shape of an object.
Recognise that things will only speed up, slow down or change direction when something else causes them to do so.
Collect and record observations and/or measurements by annotating images and completing simple tables.
Identify simple patterns in results, e.g. increasing and decreasing patterns.
Present and interpret results using tables and block graphs.

beats.say: A push or a pull is a force. A force changes how a thing moves.
A force can change a thing's shape, too. Nothing speeds up or stops by itself.
A still ball sits there for ever, unless a force acts on it.
A kick is a force. The kick starts the ball moving.
Push it along as it rolls, and it speeds up.
Push back against it, and it slows down and stops.
Tap it on the side, and it turns. It changes direction: the way it is going.
So a force can start, speed up, slow, stop or turn a thing.
Here is a toy car on a track. The distance is how far it rolls. You measure it in steps.
Push it gently. It rolls a little way: three steps.
A medium push. It rolls further: six steps.
A hard push! It rolls furthest of all: nine steps.
Same car, same floor. Only the push changed.
There is a pattern: a bigger push, a bigger move.
Write the three distances in a table. Gentle, three. Medium, six. Hard, nine.
Then build a block graph, with one block for each step.
Three blocks for gentle. Six for medium. Nine for hard.
Look at the columns. Each one is taller than the last.
That is an increasing pattern: bigger push, further roll.
An even harder push would make a taller column still.
A force can change a shape, too. Squash a sponge, and it goes flat.
Let go, and it springs back into shape.
Bend a metal paperclip. It changes shape, and it stays bent.
Squash a wooden block. Nothing happens. Your push is too small to change it.
Forces change shape, as well as movement.
Why does a rolling ball slow down? It does not run out of go.
The floor rubs against it, all the way along. That rubbing is a force called friction.
It stops at the wall, because the wall pushes back.
Nothing speeds up, slows down or turns by itself. Every change has a cause.
A push or a pull is a force. It changes movement.
A bigger push makes a bigger move. The graph shows the pattern.
A force can change a shape too, like a squashed sponge.
Nothing changes by itself. When a ball stops, ask: what made it stop?
